definitions.definition: A deep problem about what is truly real and basic in the universe.
definitions.example: If you thought your house was made of wood but found out it's actually made of Lego bricks, that would be an ontological crisis about what 'house' really means.

definitions.definition: The most basic building block of reality that everything else is made from.
definitions.example: In a video game, the code is the ontological primitive; the graphics and sounds are just different ways the code shows itself.

definitions.definition: A non-material field of pure information that is the basic stuff of reality, from which matter and energy come.
definitions.example: Think of it like the invisible operating system of a computer that makes all the programs and files possible.

definitions.definition: Something that doesn't need anything else to exist; it explains itself.
definitions.example: A self-grounding idea is like a dictionary that defines every word using only other words from the same dictionary.

definitions.definition: The underlying layer of reality made of information, not matter.
definitions.example: If reality were a movie, the informational substrate would be the digital file, not the screen or projector.

definitions.definition: Extreme situations where a general rule simplifies into a special, well-known rule.
definitions.example: At very low speeds, Einstein's theory of relativity becomes Newton's simpler physics; that's a limit case.

definitions.definition: A measure of how organized and stable a system is, from very organized (high coherence) to random (low coherence).
definitions.example: A marching band has high coherence; a crowd of people walking randomly has low coherence.

definitions.definition: Actions or functions where the order matters; swapping them changes the result.
definitions.example: Putting on socks then shoes is different from shoes then socks; those are non-commutative operations.

definitions.definition: Relating to the Christian idea of God as three distinct persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) in one being.
definitions.example: The Trinity is like a single triangle that has three different corners, each essential to the shape.

definitions.definition: The study of what exists and what it means for something to be real.
definitions.example: Asking whether numbers are real things or just ideas is an ontology question.

definitions.definition: The belief that matter is the most basic thing in the universe and everything else comes from it.
definitions.example: If you think thoughts are just brain chemicals, you believe in Material Primacy.

definitions.definition: How well a set of rules (like a recipe) can produce a complex result with very few steps.
definitions.example: A single page of code that generates an entire video game world shows high algorithmic efficiency.

definitions.definition: The problem that when you measure a quantum particle, the measuring device itself is also quantum, so you need another device to measure that, and so on forever.
definitions.example: It's like asking who watches the watchman, and then who watches the watcher of the watchman, never ending.

definitions.definition: The ability to act and make choices that doesn't depend on being made of a specific material like flesh or silicon.
definitions.example: If a robot and a human could both feel pain, that feeling would be substrate-independent.

definitions.definition: The central mathematical formula of this theory that describes how everything in reality connects.
definitions.example: Like E=mc² is a master equation for energy and matter, this is the master equation for the χ-field.

definitions.definition: A mathematical rule that stays the same value even as the system changes over time.
definitions.example: Total energy in a closed system is a conserved functional; it doesn't change no matter what happens inside.

definitions.definition: The study of how information behaves like heat and energy, with its own rules about order and disorder.
definitions.example: Erasing a computer file creates a tiny bit of heat, which is information thermodynamics in action.

definitions.definition: The path or history of a conscious being as it experiences and interacts with reality.
definitions.example: Your life from birth to now is your observer trajectory.

definitions.definition: A measure of how much disorder, fragmentation, or 'badness' increases in a system due to choices.
definitions.example: If lying makes a society more chaotic, that's an increase in Moral Entropy.

definitions.definition: A process that cannot be undone; once it happens, you can't go back.
definitions.example: Breaking an egg is irreversible; you can't un-break it.

definitions.definition: A change that doesn't follow the usual reversible rules of quantum mechanics; it's a one-way change.
definitions.example: Making a measurement in quantum mechanics is non-unitary because it forces a definite result from many possibilities.

definitions.definition: An agent or force that exists outside the system and can affect it in ways the system can't do to itself.
definitions.example: A player controlling a video game character is an external operator to the game world.

definitions.definition: The idea that a system needs exactly three distinct parts to be complete and self-consistent.
definitions.example: A three-legged stool needs all three legs to stand; two legs would fall, four would be redundant.

definitions.definition: Order or useful energy that comes from outside a system to keep it from falling apart.
definitions.example: Sunlight is external negentropy for Earth; it provides energy that keeps life organized.

definitions.definition: A final observer that ends the chain of measurements and makes reality definite.
definitions.example: If you have a line of dominoes, the terminal observer is the last one that finally falls and stops the chain.

definitions.definition: A perfect matching between two different systems where every part of one corresponds to a part of the other.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is an isomorphism to the actual subway; every station on the map matches a real station.

definitions.definition: The rules or limits at the edges of a system that determine how it behaves.
definitions.example: If you're solving a puzzle, the boundary conditions are the rules like 'pieces must fit edge to edge'.

definitions.definition: Able to be checked by doing experiments or making observations in the real world.
definitions.example: Saying 'water boils at 100°C' is empirically testable; you can heat water and check.

definitions.definition: A plan written down before an experiment that says exactly what results would prove the idea wrong.
definitions.example: Like a scientist saying 'if my new medicine doesn't help 90% of patients, I'll admit it doesn't work' before the test.

definitions.definition: The idea that how fast a quantum system becomes definite depends on how complex the observer is.
definitions.example: A simple detector might take 1 second to measure a particle, but a human might take 0.1 seconds because of their complex mind.

definitions.definition: The study of how order and organization change over time in a system.
definitions.example: Watching a sandcastle get washed away by waves is a study in coherence dynamics.

definitions.definition: A position about what we can know and how certain we can be about it.
definitions.example: Saying 'I'm 90% sure it will rain' is an epistemic stance about the weather.

definitions.definition: Relating to the nature of reality beyond what we can see or measure physically.
definitions.example: Asking whether the universe has a purpose is a metaphysical question.

definitions.definition: A perfect match between two systems that is forced by the rules, not just a coincidence.
definitions.example: If a lock and key fit perfectly because the lock was made for that key, that's a constrained isomorphism.

definitions.definition: Based on a self-evident truth that is accepted without proof.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is accepted axiomatically.

definitions.definition: The ability of simple mathematical rules to describe incredibly complex things.
definitions.example: A single equation like F=ma can describe the motion of everything from a falling apple to a rocket.

definitions.definition: The huge mismatch between the predicted and measured amount of dark energy in the universe.
definitions.example: It's like predicting your monthly allowance is $1,000,000 but actually getting $1; that's a cosmological constant problem.

definitions.definition: A difference of a factor of 10 followed by 120 zeros, an astronomically huge mismatch.
definitions.example: If you predicted 1 grain of sand but found 10^120 grains, that's the size of this discrepancy.

definitions.definition: The idea that we see a universe that supports life because if it didn't, we wouldn't be here to see it.
definitions.example: If you win the lottery, you might say 'I won because I'm lucky' (anthropic) or 'the lottery was rigged' (design).

definitions.definition: How much information is packed into a small set of rules or data.
definitions.example: A zip file has high informational efficiency because it stores a lot of data in a small space.

definitions.definition: Being the most basic kind of thing that exists, not made of anything else.
definitions.example: In this theory, information is ontologically fundamental, like atoms were once thought to be.

definitions.definition: A quantum state where a particle exists in multiple possibilities at the same time until measured.
definitions.example: A spinning coin is in superposition of heads and tails until you slap it on the table.

definitions.definition: A mathematical description of all the possible states a quantum system can be in.
definitions.example: The wave function of a cat in a box might describe both a live cat and a dead cat at the same time.

definitions.definition: When two particles are linked so that measuring one instantly affects the other, no matter how far apart they are.
definitions.example: It's like having two magic coins that always show opposite sides, even if one is on Earth and the other on Mars.

definitions.definition: The process by which a quantum system loses its weird quantum properties and becomes normal and definite.
definitions.example: A quantum particle in a vacuum might stay in superposition, but if it bumps into air molecules, decoherence makes it pick a state.

definitions.definition: Something that is always one specific way and cannot be broken down into multiple possibilities.
definitions.example: Your experience of seeing red is irreducibly definite; you don't see red and blue at the same time.

definitions.definition: The individual, subjective experiences of things like the redness of red or the pain of a headache.
definitions.example: The 'redness' you see when you look at a rose is a quale (singular of qualia).

definitions.definition: A property that appears when simple parts come together in a complex way, but isn't in the parts themselves.
definitions.example: Wetness is emergent from H2O molecules; individual molecules aren't wet, but a group of them is.

definitions.definition: A pattern of information that stays the same even if the physical stuff carrying it changes completely.
definitions.example: The same song can be on a CD, a vinyl record, or a digital file; the pattern is substrate-independent.

definitions.definition: A measure of how much a field spreads out from a point; zero divergence means nothing is lost or created.
definitions.example: If you spray water from a hose, the divergence is positive; if water flows into a drain, it's negative.

definitions.definition: The belief that only matter and energy are real, and everything else (like thoughts) comes from them.
definitions.example: A materialist ontology says your mind is just your brain's activity, not a separate thing.

definitions.definition: A field that has a single value (like temperature) at every point in space and time.
definitions.example: A weather map showing temperature at every location is a scalar field.

definitions.definition: A mathematical rule that measures how organized or ordered a configuration of the χ-field is.
definitions.example: Like a 'tidiness score' for your room; a high score means everything is in its place.

definitions.definition: A measure of how much uncertainty or information is in a set of possibilities.
definitions.example: A coin flip has 1 bit of Shannon entropy; a 6-sided die has about 2.6 bits.

definitions.definition: A quantity that stays the same over time because of a symmetry in the laws of physics.
definitions.example: Electric charge is a Noether charge; it's conserved because the laws of physics are the same everywhere.

definitions.definition: A rule that says every symmetry in nature leads to a conserved quantity.
definitions.example: Because the laws of physics don't change over time, energy is conserved (Noether's theorem).

definitions.definition: A mathematical formula that describes how different parts of a system interact, based on observed behavior.
definitions.example: Like a recipe that says 'mix flour and water' without explaining the chemistry; it describes what happens, not why.

definitions.definition: A mathematical function that summarizes all the dynamics of a physical system in one equation.
definitions.example: The Lagrangian for a pendulum tells you everything about how it swings.

definitions.definition: The Lagrangian per unit volume of space, used for fields that extend everywhere.
definitions.example: Like a recipe for every point in space, telling you how the field behaves at that point.

definitions.definition: A mathematical object that defines distances and angles in the curved fabric of spacetime.
definitions.example: In a curved space, the metric tells you how to measure a straight line, like on a globe.

definitions.definition: A term in an equation that describes how a field affects itself, like a feedback loop.
definitions.example: A crowd where people push each other; the pushing is the self-interaction potential.

definitions.definition: A direct connection between a field and gravity that goes beyond the simplest possible link.
definitions.example: Normally, a field just sits in space; non-minimal coupling means the field directly changes how space curves.

definitions.definition: A number that describes how much space is curved at a point, independent of direction.
definitions.example: On a sphere, the Ricci scalar is positive; on a saddle, it's negative; on a flat table, it's zero.

definitions.definition: A way that a field interacts with matter particles, similar to how the Higgs field gives mass.
definitions.example: Like a magnet attracting iron; the Yukawa coupling is the strength of that attraction.

definitions.definition: Mathematical formulas that derive the equations of motion from the Lagrangian.
definitions.example: If the Lagrangian is the recipe, the Euler-Lagrange equations are the instructions for how the dish cooks over time.

definitions.definition: A mathematical operator that measures how a field changes in both space and time, like a wave equation.
definitions.example: It's the 'wave detector' that tells you if a disturbance is spreading out like ripples.

definitions.definition: A system where the future is completely determined by the present; no randomness.
definitions.example: A clock is deterministic; if you know all its parts, you can predict exactly where the hands will be.

definitions.definition: A system where outcomes are random and can only be predicted as chances, not certainties.
definitions.example: Rolling a die is probabilistic; you can say there's a 1
